prompt: More and more people in developing countries are purchasing cars for the first time. What problems does this cause? What do you think is a possible solution?
intro_note: Band 7 rewrite of W8 (6.0). Keeps your two problems, your public-transport solution and your four-paragraph structure — the panel's nine rewrites applied. Highlights mark what moves each criterion.

spans.text: It is increasingly common for people in developing countries to buy a car of their own for the first time. This trend brings two serious problems —
a rise in road accidents and ever-greater consumption of fossil fuels

highlight.label: Roadmap matches the body
highlight.explanation: Your introduction listed fuel first but Body 1 treated accidents first. The preview now names the problems in the order the essay delivers them.

spans.text: Nevertheless, both problems can be eased

highlight.label: Comma splice fixed
highlight.explanation: Your thesis joined two sentences with ", nevertheless," — the recurring W3/W7/W8 splice. The adverb is kept; it just follows a full stop. Same word, legal punctuation.

spans.text: if governments make public transport a genuinely attractive alternative to driving.
The most immediate danger is a sharp increase in traffic accidents.

highlight.label: Short claim sentence
highlight.explanation: Replaces the 16-word runway ("The primary issue that people in developing nations are going to face is…") with a direct claim, so the paragraph's topic is visible instantly.

spans.text: Most first-time buyers are, by definition, inexperienced drivers, and in many developing countries licensing systems and traffic enforcement are still too weak to prepare them properly.

highlight.label: Mechanism from the prompt's own words
highlight.explanation: Your version said accidents rise "naturally" — an assertion. The proof uses exactly what the prompt supplies: first-time buyers are new drivers, and developing countries' licensing and enforcement cannot yet cope. This is the Band 7 "extended and supported" gate.

spans.text: When millions of new motorists join roads that were never designed for such volumes, collisions inevitably become more frequent. Moreover, fossil fuel consumption
is projected to climb steeply

highlight.label: Your best frame, promoted
highlight.explanation: "It is projected that…" was the most academic error-free sentence in your eight essays. The raised form ("is projected to climb") is the same structure, tightened.

spans.text: as car ownership spreads.
Unlike renewable sources such as solar or wind power

highlight.label: renewable, not "reusable"
highlight.explanation: Your W2 feedback corrected "natural energy" to renewable energy; W8 wrote "reusable energy" — the same collocation family. Renewable is the exam term, and "other" is gone because fossil fuels are not a renewable.

spans.text: , petrol cannot be produced artificially: fossil fuels take millions of years to form,
so reserves consumed at today's pace can never be replaced

highlight.label: Register lift + consequence
highlight.explanation: Replaces "they can run out if people use them a lot" — the spoken-register "a lot" from your W5 ban-list — and completes your best chain with its consequence.

spans.text: The most realistic solution is to persuade these new buyers to drive less and use public transport more. The arithmetic is simple: a single bus can
carry dozens of passengers

highlight.label: carry, not "handle"
highlight.explanation: Vehicles carry passengers ("handle several people" is a literal translation), and dozens is the honest scale of a bus — "several" undersold your own argument.

spans.text: who would otherwise travel in separate cars, so every full bus means
fewer vehicles, less congestion and lower fuel demand

highlight.label: fewer + countable, less + uncountable
highlight.explanation: Your longest-running error family ("less cars", "less traffics", "public transports") used correctly in one clause — and the sentence now explicitly serves both problems, the link your essay left implicit.

spans.text: An awareness campaign alone, however, rarely changes behaviour.

highlight.label: however, done legally
highlight.explanation: Mid-sentence "however" set off by commas inside ONE clause is fine — the fault in your conclusion was using it to weld two sentences together. Here it also concedes the campaign's limit before improving on it.

spans.text: Governments also need to make buses and subways cheaper, safer and more reliable than driving —
by subsidising fares and expanding routes in fast-growing cities

highlight.label: The behavioural mechanism
highlight.explanation: The panel's #1 rewrite: a campaign alone gives no reason to switch. Cheaper fares and better routes are the incentive that makes your solution actually map onto the problems (§8.4's rule).

spans.text: — so that leaving the car at home becomes the easier choice rather than a sacrifice.
In conclusion,
the arrival of millions of first-time car owners is likely to cost

highlight.label: The trend is the subject
highlight.explanation: Your conclusion made "people" the subject ("people purchasing cars … can result in accidents") — faulty predication. It is the trend, not the people, that causes the problems.

spans.text: lives on the road and to speed up the depletion of fossil fuels.
However, both problems

highlight.label: Splice #2 + "it" fixed together
highlight.explanation: Full stop before However kills the second splice, and "both problems" gives the reference a visible plural noun — your "it can be alleviated" pointed a singular pronoun at two problems.

spans.text: can be contained if governments invest seriously in public transport and then
campaign to make using it a normal part of daily life

highlight.label: Your campaign, kept
highlight.explanation: The campaign survives — subordinated to the investment that makes it credible, so the conclusion no longer shrinks your solution to the means alone.
